title: Claude Certified Developer — Foundations
disclaimer: Practice questions authored from the official exam guide. These are NOT official exam items.

questions.prompt: Objective 1.1 covers decision criteria for choosing between two ways of structuring work. Which pair of approaches do those criteria compare?

options.text: The Claude Agent SDK and agent loops
A fixed workflow and an autonomous agent
Self-hosted and Anthropic-hosted deployment

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options because the slice names exactly one decision axis (workflow versus agent); the two distractors are the other named pairings from objective 1.2, so each option tests a real boundary rather than padding. Two would have hidden the 1.1/1.2 boundary that makes the item worth asking.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the misconception that the Agent SDK and hand-rolled loops are the architecture decision; they are construction methods listed under 1.2, not the workflow-versus-agent choice.
distractorRationale.c: Probes confusion between architectural choice and deployment choice; self-hosted versus Anthropic-hosted is a managed deployment model under 1.2.

explanation.correct: Objective 1.1 (Agent Architecture) explicitly includes the decision criteria for using a workflow versus an agent as part of the architectural principles, patterns, and tradeoffs it measures.

whyWrong.a: The Claude Agent SDK and custom agent loops and harnesses are construction methods named under objective 1.2, not the architectural decision 1.1 describes.
whyWrong.c: Self-hosted versus Anthropic-hosted is a managed agent deployment model named under objective 1.2, not the workflow-versus-agent architectural decision.

explanation.analogy: Architecture picks the shape of the solution (fixed steps or autonomous judgement); construction and deployment pick the machinery and where it runs.
explanation.takeaway: Objective 1.1 is about choosing between a workflow and an agent; the SDK, loops, and hosting models belong to objective 1.2.
explanation.deepDive: The objective also names the structure of manager/supervisor hierarchies and the role of subagents in improving task execution, so 1.1 is about architecture decisions rather than about the tools that build them.

questions.prompt: Which of these belongs to Agent Architecture (objective 1.1) rather than to Agent Construction with Claude (objective 1.2)?

options.text: Tradeoffs between architectural choices for agents and workflows
The Claude Agent SDK
Managed agent deployment models, self-hosted versus Anthropic-hosted

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: one genuine 1.1 item plus the two most confusable 1.2 items (a named tool and a named deployment choice). A fourth would have been another 1.2 restatement with no new discrimination.

distractorRationale.b: Probes the misconception that a framework or SDK is an architectural concern; the guide files it as a construction tool under 1.2.
distractorRationale.c: Probes confusion between where a system runs and how it is shaped; hosting choices are a 1.2 concern.

explanation.correct: Objective 1.1 measures the principles, patterns, and tradeoffs of agent and workflow architecture, so the tradeoffs themselves are squarely inside its scope.

whyWrong.b: The Claude Agent SDK is named under objective 1.2 as a tool for constructing agents, not as an architecture concern.
whyWrong.c: Self-hosted versus Anthropic-hosted deployment models are named under objective 1.2 as construction and deployment choices, not as architecture.

explanation.takeaway: Tradeoffs, hierarchy structure, and subagent roles sit in 1.1; the SDK, custom loops, deployment models, and hooks sit in 1.2.
explanation.deepDive: A reliable test for the boundary: if the sentence would still be true with Claude replaced by another model, it is architecture; if it depends on Claude's tooling, it is construction.

questions.prompt: A team is still deciding whether a task should run as a fixed workflow or as an autonomous agent. Which area of the guide should they start with?

options.text: The decision criteria for using a workflow versus an agent (1.1)
Hooks and other mechanisms for deterministic actions (1.2)
Abstraction frameworks such as LangGraph (1.3)

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options, one per objective in the domain, so the item doubles as a scope map of Domain 1. A fourth option would add no new discrimination because the slice offers only three distinct construction/architecture areas.

distractorRationale.b: Probes the misconception that deterministic mechanisms decide architecture; hooks are how you build an agent, not how you choose between a workflow and an agent.
distractorRationale.c: Probes picking a framework before making the architectural decision; the framework layer comes after the choice of approach.

explanation.correct: The guide places the decision criteria for using a workflow versus an agent inside Agent Architecture (1.1), which is exactly the question this team is asking.

whyWrong.b: Hooks for deterministic actions are a construction mechanism under 1.2. They say how an agent performs a fixed step, not whether the overall design should be a workflow or an agent.
whyWrong.c: Abstraction frameworks such as Strands, LangGraph, and PydanticAI are listed under 1.3 for building agents and workflows for multi-step tasks. Choosing a framework before settling the architecture reverses the order of decisions.

explanation.takeaway: Decide architecture first (1.1), then construction mechanisms (1.2), then the pattern or framework layer (1.3).
explanation.deepDive: Scenario items like this are common in this exam because each objective answers a different question: 1.1 asks what shape the solution takes, 1.2 asks what builds it, 1.3 asks which pattern or framework organises it.

questions.prompt: Objective 1.2 lists managed agent deployment models. Which pair of deployment models does it name?

options.text: Self-hosted and Anthropic-hosted
Client-side and serverless

questions.optionCountRationale: Two options because the slice names this pair explicitly and completely as a binary distinction. The learning objective is recall of the named pair, so a third or fourth invented option would add no discrimination.

distractorRationale.b: Probes a plausible-sounding but unnamed hosting split; the guide names self-hosted versus Anthropic-hosted, not client-side versus serverless.

explanation.correct: Agent Construction with Claude (1.2) names managed agent deployment models as self-hosted versus Anthropic-hosted.

whyWrong.b: Client-side versus serverless is not a pair the guide names. The deployment axis in objective 1.2 is who runs the agent: your own infrastructure or Anthropic.

explanation.analogy: Self-hosted is running the agent on your own machine or infrastructure; Anthropic-hosted is letting Anthropic run it.
explanation.takeaway: The managed deployment axis in 1.2 is self-hosted versus Anthropic-hosted.

questions.prompt: Which mechanism does Agent Construction with Claude (1.2) name for taking deterministic actions inside an agent?

options.text: Context-window management, which is a design pattern listed under 1.3
Session management, which is a Claude Code feature listed under 3.1
Hooks, which are named under 1.2 for deterministic actions

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the correct term plus the two nearest named mechanisms from adjacent objectives (1.3 pattern, 3.1 feature), each of which is a real item in the guide and a genuine confusion. Three keeps every option earn its place.

distractorRationale.a: Probes confusing a design pattern with a construction mechanism; context-window management is listed among the common agent design patterns in 1.3.
distractorRationale.b: Probes pulling a Claude Code feature into a general agent-construction question; session management belongs to objective 3.1.

explanation.correct: Objective 1.2 lists hooks among the methods, tools, and platforms for constructing Claude agents, specifically for deterministic actions.

whyWrong.a: Context-window management is one of the common agent design patterns named under objective 1.3, not the mechanism for deterministic actions.
whyWrong.b: Session management is a Claude Code feature named under objective 3.1. It has no role in general agent construction.

explanation.analogy: The model decides the judgement calls; hooks are the fixed steps that always run the same way.
explanation.takeaway: Hooks are 1.2's answer to deterministic behaviour inside an agent.
explanation.deepDive: Objective 1.2 also names the Claude Agent SDK and custom agent loops and harnesses, so hooks sit alongside tools and loops as construction choices.

questions.prompt: Objective 1.2 names methods, tools, and platforms for constructing Claude agents. Which group belongs to that list?

options.text: The Claude Agent SDK and custom agent loops and harnesses
Strands, LangGraph, and PydanticAI
Rules, Skills, Commands, and Agent Memory

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options, each a named list from a different objective of the guide (1.2, 1.3, 3.1), so the item tests the domain map as well as recall of 1.2. No fourth group exists in the slice to add.

distractorRationale.b: Probes confusion between construction tools and abstraction frameworks; Strands, LangGraph, and PydanticAI are named under 1.3.
distractorRationale.c: Probes pulling Claude Code's core components into an agent-construction list; Rules, Skills, Commands, and Agent Memory are named under 3.1.

explanation.correct: Objective 1.2 names the Claude Agent SDK and custom agent loops and harnesses as methods, tools, and platforms for constructing Claude agents.

whyWrong.b: Strands, LangGraph, and PydanticAI are the agentic abstraction frameworks named under objective 1.3, a different layer from construction tools.
whyWrong.c: Rules, Skills, Commands, and Agent Memory are Claude Code core components named under objective 3.1, not general agent construction tools.

explanation.takeaway: 1.2 construction = the Agent SDK, custom loops and harnesses, hosting models, and hooks; 1.3 = patterns and frameworks.
explanation.deepDive: Keeping the three layers straight is the fastest way to answer scope questions in Domain 1: architecture (1.1), construction (1.2), patterns and frameworks (1.3).

questions.prompt: A release pipeline needs a validation step that runs the same way every time, with no model deciding whether it happens. Which objective 1.2 mechanism fits?

options.text: A custom agent loop that lets the model choose the next step
Hooks, which 1.2 names for deterministic actions
Session management from Claude Code, listed under 3.1

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: a same-objective tool, the correct mechanism, and one cross-objective term. Each distractor represents a distinct way a candidate might misread the phrase deterministic action, so a fourth option would be redundant.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the opposite mental model: a custom agent loop is where the model chooses the next action, which is exactly what the pipeline must avoid.
distractorRationale.c: Probes reaching for Claude Code tooling when the requirement is about agent construction; session management is a 3.1 feature and does not make a step deterministic.

explanation.correct: Objective 1.2 names hooks as the mechanism for deterministic actions, which matches a validation step that must run identically every time.

whyWrong.a: A custom agent loop is explicitly a place where the agent decides what to do next. That is the opposite of a fixed, always-identical step.
whyWrong.c: Session management is a Claude Code feature under objective 3.1. It controls interaction sessions, not whether a given action is deterministic.

explanation.takeaway: When an action must always happen the same way, the guide points to hooks, not to an agent loop.
explanation.deepDive: The distinction matters in pipeline and tooling scenarios: model-driven loops are for open-ended work, hooks are for the fixed, auditable steps around it.

questions.prompt: Which of these is listed as a common agent design pattern in objective 1.3?

options.text: Strands, one of the agentic abstraction frameworks
PydanticAI, one of the agentic abstraction frameworks
Context-window management, one of the common design patterns

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options separating the pattern list from the framework list inside objective 1.3. The two distractors are both real named frameworks, so the item tests the pattern/framework split rather than general recall.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the misconception that every named item in 1.3 is a framework; Strands belongs to the abstraction framework list.
distractorRationale.b: Probes the same pattern/framework confusion as option a from a different named example, so a candidate who half-remembers the list still has to classify it.

explanation.correct: Objective 1.3 lists the common agent design patterns as tool-use loops, sub-agents, memory, and context-window management, so context-window management is a pattern.

whyWrong.a: Strands is named in objective 1.3 as an agentic abstraction framework, not as a design pattern.
whyWrong.b: PydanticAI is named in objective 1.3 as an agentic abstraction framework, not as a design pattern.

explanation.analogy: Patterns are the recurring shapes a solution takes; frameworks are the libraries that implement them.
explanation.takeaway: In 1.3, patterns are tool-use loops, sub-agents, memory, and context-window management; frameworks are Strands, LangGraph, and PydanticAI.
explanation.deepDive: Both groups appear in the same objective because the guide treats them as two layers of the same job: building agents and workflows for multi-step tasks.

questions.prompt: A team is choosing an abstraction layer for building agents and workflows for a multi-step research task. Which set is the framework list in objective 1.3?

options.text: Hooks, agent loops, and harnesses
Strands, LangGraph, and PydanticAI
Rules, Skills, Commands, and Agent Memory

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options, one per layer of the guide (1.2 construction, 1.3 frameworks, 3.1 Claude Code components). Three named groups exist in the slice; a fourth would have to be invented.

distractorRationale.a: Probes confusing construction mechanisms with frameworks; hooks, loops, and harnesses are 1.2 items.
distractorRationale.c: Probes confusing Claude Code components with agentic frameworks; Rules, Skills, Commands, and Agent Memory are 3.1 items.

explanation.correct: Objective 1.3 names Strands, LangGraph, and PydanticAI as the agentic abstraction frameworks for building agents and workflows for multi-step tasks.

whyWrong.a: Hooks and custom agent loops and harnesses are named under objective 1.2 as construction methods, not as abstraction frameworks.
whyWrong.c: Rules, Skills, Commands, and Agent Memory are Claude Code core components named under objective 3.1, not agentic frameworks.

explanation.takeaway: The framework layer in 1.3 is Strands, LangGraph, and PydanticAI, used for agents and workflows handling multi-step tasks.
explanation.deepDive: The scenario matters because the guide ties frameworks specifically to multi-step work, which is why a multi-step research task is the natural fit for this layer.

questions.prompt: The guide says agentic abstraction frameworks are for building agents and workflows for a particular kind of task. Which kind?

options.text: Tasks a single model call completes without any orchestration
Model selection experiments trading cost against quality
Multi-step tasks that agents and workflows are built to handle

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the stated purpose plus two realistic but wrong framings (no orchestration needed, and a tuning task). Both distractors correspond to real categories elsewhere in the guide, so they earn their place.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the belief that frameworks only matter for complicated work; the guide ties frameworks to multi-step tasks, which is the opposite of the no-orchestration case.
distractorRationale.b: Probes confusing framework selection with model selection, which is a different area of the guide entirely.

explanation.correct: The guide states that agentic abstraction frameworks are used for building agents and workflows for multi-step tasks.

whyWrong.a: If no orchestration is needed, there is no multi-step task and no need for an agent or workflow framework.
whyWrong.b: Trading cost against quality is model selection, not the stated purpose of agentic abstraction frameworks.

explanation.takeaway: Frameworks in 1.3 exist for multi-step tasks, which is exactly where single-call approaches stop being enough.
explanation.deepDive: Linking the framework layer back to the pattern list: tool-use loops, sub-agents, memory, and context-window management are the patterns a framework helps you express for multi-step work.

questions.prompt: Which two categories of requirements does objective 2.1 (Understanding Requirements) measure?

options.text: Functional and infrastructure requirements
Functional and non-functional requirements

questions.optionCountRationale: Two options: the slice names exactly these two categories, and the only live confusion is between 'infrastructure' and the conventional 'non-functional' label. A third option would have to be invented rather than sourced.

distractorRationale.b: Probes the widespread assumption that requirement types split functional vs non-functional, which is standard requirements-engineering vocabulary but not the pair this objective names.

explanation.correct: Objective 2.1 is described as functional and infrastructure requirements, derived from business requirements and solution architecture.

whyWrong.b: 'Non-functional' is the conventional industry term, but the guide's wording for 2.1 pairs functional with infrastructure, not with non-functional.

explanation.takeaway: Objective 2.1 measures functional and infrastructure requirements.
explanation.deepDive: 2.1 carries 3.4% of the exam, the second-smallest skill in Domain 2. Know the exact pair of words and the two inputs; the guide gives no detail beyond that single sentence.

questions.prompt: Per objective 2.1, what are the functional and infrastructure requirements based on?

options.text: User research sessions and legacy code audits
Business requirements and solution architecture
Project budgets and vendor contracts

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the two inputs the slice names, plus two plausible discovery sources that match neither stated input and let the item test the direction of the requirements chain.

distractorRationale.a: Probes treating discovery activities as the basis of requirements; the slice names business requirements and solution architecture as the basis, not research or audits.
distractorRationale.c: Probes treating commercial constraints as the basis of requirements, which the slice does not list as an input to 2.1.

explanation.correct: The slice states that 2.1 covers functional and infrastructure requirements based on business requirements and solution architecture.

whyWrong.a: User research and code audits are discovery techniques; the guide does not name them as the basis for 2.1's requirement categories.
whyWrong.c: Budgets and vendor contracts are not named in 2.1; the two stated bases are business requirements and solution architecture.

explanation.takeaway: Business requirements and solution architecture are the inputs; functional and infrastructure requirements are what 2.1 measures.
explanation.deepDive: Keep the direction of the chain straight: business requirements and solution architecture feed into 2.1, and 2.1 produces the functional and infrastructure requirement sets.

questions.prompt: Objective 2.2 (Systems Life Cycle) covers systems life cycle management used to do what?

options.text: Design, build, deploy, and decommission IT systems
Develop, implement, operate, and maintain IT systems
Plan, analyze, control, and measure project work
Discover, define, deliver, and support product work

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options: the slice enumerates exactly four verbs, and each distractor is a different widely used lifecycle phrasing a candidate could import from elsewhere. The exact-wording recall is what earns the extra option.

distractorRationale.a: Probes substituting a design-build-deploy-retire delivery pipeline for the develop-implement-operate-maintain set the guide states.
distractorRationale.c: Probes confusing systems life cycle management with project management process groups.
distractorRationale.d: Probes confusing systems life cycle management with a product discovery and delivery framing.

explanation.correct: The guide describes 2.2 as systems life cycle management concepts and frameworks used to develop, implement, operate, and maintain IT systems.

whyWrong.a: Design, build, deploy, and decommission is a different phase set; the guide's wording is develop, implement, operate, and maintain.
whyWrong.c: Plan, analyze, control, and measure describes project management activities, which the slice does not name for 2.2.
whyWrong.d: Discover, define, deliver, and support is a product framing; the slice names lifecycle verbs applied to IT systems.

explanation.takeaway: Systems life cycle management in 2.2 means develop, implement, operate, and maintain.
explanation.deepDive: 2.2 is 2.8% of the exam, the smallest skill in Domain 2, and the guide gives it a single sentence. There is nothing further to study here beyond the four verbs and the fact that the object is IT systems.

questions.prompt: Which Domain 2 objective covers systems life cycle management concepts and frameworks?

options.text: Objective 2.1, Understanding Requirements
Objective 2.2, Systems Life Cycle
Objective 2.4, Software Engineering Foundations

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the named objective plus its two nearest Domain 2 neighbours. The boundary being tested is exactly three-way, so a fourth option would add nothing.

distractorRationale.a: Probes swapping requirements work (2.1) with lifecycle work (2.2); both sit in the same domain and are easy to blur.
distractorRationale.c: Probes swapping lifecycle scope (2.2) with engineering practice (2.4), which share the word 'systems' in the guide's phrasing.

explanation.correct: Objective 2.2 is titled Systems Life Cycle and is described as systems life cycle management concepts and frameworks.

whyWrong.a: 2.1 is Understanding Requirements, covering functional and infrastructure requirements, not lifecycle frameworks.
whyWrong.c: 2.4 is Software Engineering Foundations, covering practices such as REST APIs, version control, and code review, not lifecycle frameworks.

explanation.takeaway: Objective 2.2 is the systems life cycle objective; 2.1 is requirements and 2.4 is engineering practice.
explanation.deepDive: The guide defines each Domain 2 skill with one sentence, so scope matching is the only defensible question type for the lighter objectives. Get the objective-to-topic map right before worrying about detail.

Messages API data access patterns
Model version pinning and prompt versioning
Invoking Claude through third-party vendors

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options with three correct: 2.3 is the longest enumeration in the domain, so a select-all item tests the named scope directly rather than compressing it into one answer. The single wrong option is taken from 2.6 so it is clearly defensible.

distractorRationale.c: Probes carrying configuration concerns from 2.6 into the API mechanics list; both appear in Domain 2, but in different objectives.

explanation.correct: Objective 2.3 names streaming, batch API use, Messages API data access patterns, and invoking Claude through third-party vendors among its listed topics.

whyWrong.c: Model version pinning and prompt versioning are named under 2.6 Configuration Management, not under Claude API Mechanics.

explanation.takeaway: 2.3's list is messages, tools, streaming, vision, thinking, caching, third-party vendors, Messages API data access patterns, and batch API use.
explanation.deepDive: 2.3 is 6.8% of the exam. The same sentence also names 'tradeoffs between realtime and batch API selection', the only part of the objective framed as a decision rather than a topic.

questions.prompt: Objective 2.3 explicitly names tradeoffs between which two API selection modes?

options.text: Streaming and batch
Realtime and batch

questions.optionCountRationale: Two options: the guide's phrase is a single explicit pair. The only meaningful confusion is streaming, which 2.3 lists as a topic but not as the other side of this tradeoff.

distractorRationale.a: Probes treating streaming — a delivery mode 2.3 does list — as the counterpart in the stated selection tradeoff; the guide pairs realtime with batch.

explanation.correct: The guide states that 2.3 covers 'tradeoffs between realtime and batch API selection'.

whyWrong.a: Streaming is named in 2.3 as a topic, but the tradeoff the guide states is between realtime and batch API selection.

explanation.takeaway: The API selection tradeoff 2.3 names is realtime versus batch.
explanation.deepDive: Streaming, vision, thinking, and caching are listed as API topics. Realtime and batch are the pair you are told to weigh when choosing how to run a workload.

questions.prompt: Which grouping belongs to objective 2.3 (Claude API Mechanics) rather than objective 2.4 (Software Engineering Foundations)?

options.text: Messages, tools, and streaming behavior
REST APIs, JSON, and version control
Code review and refactoring at small and large scale

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: one grouping from 2.3 and two groupings the slice explicitly assigns to 2.4. The boundary between Claude API behaviour and general engineering practice is the whole point of the item.

distractorRationale.b: Probes attributing REST and JSON to the Claude API objective; the slice places both under Software Engineering Foundations.
distractorRationale.c: Probes attributing code review and refactoring to the API objective; both are named under 2.4.

explanation.correct: Messages, tools, and streaming are named in 2.3's list of Claude API behaviour and mechanics.

whyWrong.b: REST APIs, JSON, and version control are named in 2.4, not in 2.3, even though REST APIs are also APIs.
whyWrong.c: Code review and small- and large-scale refactoring are named in 2.4, not in 2.3.

explanation.takeaway: 2.3 is Claude API behaviour; REST, JSON, version control, code review, and refactoring belong to 2.4.
explanation.deepDive: 2.4 is 7.4% of the exam, the second-heaviest skill in Domain 2, so expect repeated pressure on this boundary. The guide separates Claude-specific API mechanics from general software engineering practice even though both mention APIs.

questions.prompt: Which group of practices does objective 2.4 (Software Engineering Foundations) name?

options.text: REST APIs and JSON interchange
Model selection, token cost, and latency control
Asynchronous programming, version control, and code review
Content boundaries and session hygiene

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options: the slice enumerates 2.4's practices, so a multi-item correct grouping is supportable and keeps the option lengths comparable. Each distractor comes from a different Domain 2 area or from a subject 2.4 never names.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the 2.3 versus 2.4 boundary from the other side: REST and JSON are named in 2.4, so this group is real but belongs to a different objective than the correct answer.
distractorRationale.b: Probes confusing core engineering practice with cost and performance engineering, which 2.4 does not name.
distractorRationale.d: Probes confusing engineering practice with the design concerns that 2.5 names.

explanation.correct: Objective 2.4 names core software engineering principles and practices, including asynchronous programming, version control, SDLC integration, and code review.

whyWrong.a: REST APIs and JSON are genuinely part of 2.4, but this group is smaller than the set the objective names and does not include the distinguishing practices such as asynchronous programming and code review.
whyWrong.b: Model selection, token cost, and latency control are not named in 2.4's practice list.
whyWrong.d: Content boundaries and session hygiene are named under 2.5 Claude Application Design.

explanation.takeaway: 2.4 names REST APIs, JSON, asynchronous programming, version control, SDLC integration, code review, and refactoring at both scales.
explanation.deepDive: Option A is deliberately a true-but-partial reading of 2.4; the exam tests whether you can reproduce the whole enumeration rather than latch onto two familiar words.

questions.prompt: Objective 2.4 names refactoring at which scales?

options.text: Both small and large scale
Small scale only, not system-wide

questions.optionCountRationale: Two options: the slice's hyphenated phrase 'small- and large-scale refactoring' makes this a clean binary scope test. A third option would be padding on a single phrase.

distractorRationale.b: Probes the belief that large-scale refactoring is a separate discipline kept outside a software engineering foundations objective.

explanation.correct: The guide lists 'small- and large-scale refactoring' among objective 2.4's core software engineering practices.

whyWrong.b: The guide explicitly names large-scale refactoring alongside small-scale, so restricting it to small scale contradicts the objective's wording.

explanation.takeaway: 2.4 covers refactoring at both small and large scale.
explanation.deepDive: The hyphenation in 'small- and large-scale refactoring' is the guide's own construction — both scales sit inside the objective, and neither is implied rather than stated.

questions.prompt: Objective 2.4 lists 'SDLC integration' among its practices. Which broader process does that refer to?

options.text: The systems development life cycle
The Claude API's realtime call path

questions.optionCountRationale: Two options: SDLC is a single named practice in 2.4 and the acronym expands unambiguously; the only plausible confusion is the API-mechanics objective. A third option would be invention.

distractorRationale.b: Probes reading 'SDLC' as something inside the Claude API stack; 2.3 owns the realtime call path, and SDLC is a development-process term.

explanation.correct: SDLC refers to the systems development life cycle, which is the process objective 2.4 names when it lists SDLC integration among core software engineering practices.

whyWrong.b: The realtime API call path is part of 2.3's API mechanics, not what SDLC integration in 2.4 refers to.

explanation.takeaway: SDLC integration in 2.4 means software engineering practice tied to the systems development life cycle.
explanation.deepDive: Do not confuse the two lifecycle-adjacent items in Domain 2: 2.4 integrates engineering practices with the development life cycle, while 2.2 is about systems life cycle management concepts and frameworks for IT systems.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. Objective 2.5 says Claude interprets instructions across which interfaces?

The API and SDKs

Content boundaries, schema design, and session hygiene
CLAUDE.md files, settings.json, and model version pinning

questions.prompt: A team wants instructions to behave consistently in Claude Code and claude.ai. Which Domain 2 objective governs that design choice?

options.text: Designing how Claude interprets instructions across interfaces
Pinning the model version a component runs on

questions.prompt: You send the same completion prompt twice with identical input and get back two differently worded completions that both satisfy the request. Which LLM fundamental does this illustrate?

options.text: Tokens — the model reads and writes text in token units.
Non-determinism — identical input can yield different output.
Context window — the amount of text the model can consider.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options give one genuine distractor per adjacent fundamental in the same list — tokens and the context window are the two that get conflated with non-determinism — with no padding.

distractorRationale.a: Probes conflating the unit text is processed in with the repeatability of the output; tokenisation explains representation, not why two runs differ.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the misconception that a fixed or large context window makes generation reproducible; the window bounds how much input is considered, not output variance.

explanation.correct: Domain 5.1 lists non-determinism as a core LLM fundamental. The same request can come back differently worded across runs because output is produced next-token by next-token under sampling rather than retrieved from a fixed stored answer.

whyWrong.a: Tokens describe the units text is broken into for processing. Two runs using the same tokens can still differ, so tokenisation does not explain the difference you saw.
whyWrong.c: The context window limits how much text the model can take in at once. Holding that limit steady, or raising it, does not make the output repeatable.

explanation.analogy: Like asking the same person the same question twice: both answers are usually right, but rarely word-for-word identical.
explanation.takeaway: Same input can still produce different output — that is non-determinism, not a malfunction.

options.text: Context window — how much text the model can hold at once.

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the mechanism asked about sits beside two closely related fundamentals in the same list, and a binary choice would leave the most confusable term unaddressed.

whyWrong.a: The context window bounds how much text the model can take in at once. It says nothing about the order in which the answer is produced.
whyWrong.b: Sampling is about choice among candidates. Producing the response one token at a time is next-token generation, a distinct item in the same list.

explanation.analogy: Autocomplete run for a whole paragraph, not a sentence pulled finished off a shelf.

questions.prompt: Which set of topics does the Developer Foundations guide place under 7.1, AI Application Security?

options.text: Model routing, prompt caching, and token budget management
Data privacy and security best practices, from prompt injection to PII handling
Content policy, guardrail layering, and secure-by-design principles

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: one list that matches 7.1 and two lists the guide places under other objectives (7.2 and the model/context work in other domains). The boundary is the learning point, so a fourth option would only add noise.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the common mistake of treating efficiency topics as security topics; routing, caching, and token budgets are named elsewhere in the guide, not in 7.1.
distractorRationale.c: Probes confusion between AI application security (7.1) and guardrails with secure-by-design (7.2); content policy, guardrail layering, identity and access management, and least privilege are all named under 7.2.

explanation.correct: 7.1 is data privacy and security best practices: prompt injection awareness and mitigation, jailbreak defense, untrusted input handling, data leakage prevention, and PII handling, plus ensuring authentication, authorization, confidentiality, privacy, and integrity.

whyWrong.a: Routing, caching, and token budget management are cost and performance concerns; the slice names none of them under AI Application Security.
whyWrong.c: Content policy, guardrail layering, and secure-by-design principles (privacy, identity and access management, least privilege) are the two halves of 7.2, Guardrails and Safe Deployment.

explanation.takeaway: 7.1 is the data-privacy and application-security skill: injection, jailbreaks, untrusted input, leakage, and PII.
explanation.analogy: Think of 7.1 as the alarm system inside the building; 7.2 is the building policy and the way the doors are designed.

questions.prompt: A customer-support assistant will read free-text messages pasted in by end users. Which pair of concerns does 7.1 name as in scope for this?

options.text: Prompt injection awareness and mitigation, and jailbreak defense
Guardrail layering and content policy for safe deployment
Hooks that stop destructive actions inside Claude applications

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the 7.1 pair named in the slice, plus the two adjacent security mechanisms a candidate is most likely to grab instead. Both distractors are real skills in this domain, just wrong ones for this prompt.

distractorRationale.b: Probes the swap between detecting bad input (7.1) and controlling what the deployed system may output (7.2).
distractorRationale.c: Probes the swap between input-side defense (7.1) and the runtime interception mechanism named under 7.3, Claude Hooks.

explanation.correct: 7.1 explicitly names prompt injection awareness and mitigation and jailbreak defense, which is exactly the risk when untrusted user text reaches a Claude application.

whyWrong.b: Guardrail layering and content policy belong to 7.2's safe and responsible deployment practices; they shape deployment policy rather than defending the application against injection attempts in its input.
whyWrong.c: Hooks are named in 7.3 as a way to prevent destructive actions within Claude applications, which is a different control from defending the input path.

explanation.takeaway: Untrusted user text is a 7.1 problem: prompt injection awareness and mitigation, plus jailbreak defense.
explanation.deepDive: The slice also lists untrusted input handling and data leakage prevention under the same objective. The slice does not define how injection is detected or blocked, so do not expect mechanism-level detail.

questions.prompt: Past injection and jailbreak concerns, which group of properties does 7.1 say an application should ensure?

options.text: Latency, accuracy, and context capacity at inference time
Availability, scalability, and cost efficiency once deployed
Authentication, authorization, confidentiality, privacy, and integrity

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the exact list from the slice plus two plausible-sounding non-security property groups that candidates might substitute from performance and cost reasoning.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the confusion between model-performance properties and the security properties 7.1 asks you to ensure.
distractorRationale.b: Probes reading availability and scalability as security requirements; the slice names confidentiality and integrity instead, and says nothing about operational efficiency here.

explanation.correct: 7.1 ends with ensuring authentication, authorization, confidentiality, privacy, and integrity. Those five words are the recall target for the tail of the objective.

whyWrong.a: Latency, accuracy, and context capacity are model-selection and optimization concerns, not the security properties listed under 7.1.
whyWrong.b: Availability and scalability are operational concerns, and cost efficiency is a token-management topic; none appear in 7.1's list.

explanation.takeaway: The five properties 7.1 names are authentication, authorization, confidentiality, privacy, and integrity.

questions.prompt: Which pair does the guide list as a secure-by-design principle under 7.2, Guardrails and Safe Deployment?

options.text: Identity and access management, and least privilege
Jailbreak defense and untrusted input handling

questions.optionCountRationale: Two options, because the slice draws a clean boundary: each side is a phrase the guide uses verbatim under one of the two objectives, so a third option would blur rather than sharpen the distinction being tested.

distractorRationale.b: Probes the most common mix-up in this domain: application-level defenses against hostile input (7.1) versus design-time access principles (7.2).

explanation.correct: 7.2 splits into two halves: safe and responsible deployment practices (content policy, guardrail layering) and secure-by-design principles, which the slice names as privacy, identity and access management, and least privilege.

whyWrong.b: Jailbreak defense and untrusted input handling are named under 7.1, AI Application Security. They defend the running application; 7.2's secure-by-design principles are privacy, identity and access management, and least privilege.

explanation.takeaway: Guardrails and deployment policy are 7.2; defenses against hostile input are 7.1.
explanation.deepDive: Both objectives appear in the same domain and both mention privacy. The reliable split is the emphasis: 7.1 is defending the application, 7.2 is the deployment and design posture.

questions.prompt: Which of these does the guide name as a safe and responsible deployment practice under 7.2?

options.text: Prompt injection awareness and data leakage prevention
Communication over stdio, sockets, and client vs. server
A content policy together with guardrail layering

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the pair the slice names for 7.2 deployment practices, plus one 7.1 phrase pair and one 8.2 phrase that candidates might borrow from neighbouring objectives.

distractorRationale.a: Probes pulling application-security phrases into a question about deployment practice.
distractorRationale.b: Probes confusion with the MCP communication patterns in 8.2, which a candidate may associate with 'deployment' generally.

explanation.correct: 7.2 names content policy and guardrail layering as its safe and responsible deployment practices, alongside secure-by-design principles.

whyWrong.a: Prompt injection awareness and data leakage prevention are named under 7.1, AI Application Security, not as deployment practices.
whyWrong.b: stdio, sockets, and client vs. server are the MCP communication patterns listed under 8.2, MCP Server Development.

explanation.takeaway: For 7.2 remember the pair: content policy and guardrail layering.

questions.prompt: According to the guide, what are Claude hooks for inside a Claude application?

options.text: Managing credentials and API keys across environments
Acting as guardrails and safety controls that block destructive actions
Writing tool descriptions and handling errors when tools are called

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: the slice's own sentence for 7.3 plus the two neighbouring skills a candidate is likely to confuse it with, each of which is a real objective in this deck.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the confusion between hooks (7.3) and secret and credential management (7.4), which are adjacent items in the same domain.
distractorRationale.c: Probes the confusion between hooks (7.3) and tool implementation work in 8.1, where error handling and tool descriptions are named.

explanation.correct: The slice describes 7.3 as leveraging hooks for guardrails and safety controls to prevent destructive actions within Claude applications.

whyWrong.a: Secrets, credentials, and API keys across development and production are the subject of 7.4, Identity, Secrets, and Key Management, not of hooks.
whyWrong.c: Tool description writing and error handling are named under 8.1, Tool Implementation. Hooks are described in terms of safety controls, not tool authoring.

explanation.takeaway: Hooks are the safety controls that prevent destructive actions inside a Claude application.
explanation.deepDive: 7.3 is the smallest objective in the domain at 1.0% of the exam and has only one sentence of detail. Learn that one sentence and do not import hook events or configuration syntax.

questions.prompt: Which statement matches 7.4, Identity, Secrets, and Key Management?

options.text: It covers secrets, credentials, and API keys across development and production environments
It covers content policy and guardrail layering for safe and responsible deployment
It covers prompt injection awareness, jailbreak defense, and untrusted input handling

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options of near-identical length: one 7.4 statement and the one-line summaries of 7.2 and 7.1, so the item tests scope recall rather than phrasing clues.

distractorRationale.b: Probes the adjacent-objective mix-up between deployment guardrails (7.2) and credential and identity management (7.4).
distractorRationale.c: Probes the mix-up between application security against hostile input (7.1) and management of the credentials and identities you already trust.

explanation.correct: 7.4 is managing secrets, credentials, and API keys across Claude development and production environments, including identity validation and authentication, access approval and level verification, and authorized access monitoring.

whyWrong.b: Content policy and guardrail layering are the safe and responsible deployment practices named under 7.2.
whyWrong.c: Prompt injection awareness, jailbreak defense, and untrusted input handling are named under 7.1, AI Application Security.

explanation.takeaway: 7.4 spans the whole credential lifecycle: secrets and API keys across environments, plus validating, approving, and monitoring access.
explanation.deepDive: The slice treats access as a lifecycle for 7.4, not a single step: identity validation and authentication, then access approval and level verification, then authorized access monitoring.

questions.prompt: Before a release, a team must confirm that only approved people, at the access level they should hold, are reaching the production application. Which objective covers that?

options.text: 7.1, because it covers untrusted input handling and data leakage prevention
7.2, because identity and access management is a secure-by-design principle
7.4, because it covers access approval, level verification, and access monitoring

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options, one per candidate objective in the domain, because the item turns on picking the right objective and the three choices make that boundary explicit and equally long.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the confusion between defending against untrusted input (7.1) and controlling who is allowed in (7.4).
distractorRationale.b: Probes the closest real overlap in the domain: 7.2 does name identity and access management, so the candidate must notice that 7.4 is the one naming approval, level verification, and monitoring.

explanation.correct: 7.4 names access approval and level verification along with authorized access monitoring, which matches confirming who is approved, at what level, and watching that authorized access.

whyWrong.a: 7.1 is about hostile or untrusted input reaching the model: prompt injection, jailbreaks, untrusted input handling, and leakage. It says nothing about approving or monitoring users.
whyWrong.b: 7.2 does name identity and access management as a secure-by-design principle, so this is a genuine near-miss; however, the specific activities in the prompt, approving access, verifying the level granted, and monitoring authorized access, are the words 7.4 uses.

explanation.takeaway: Approving an access level and monitoring who uses it is 7.4; 7.2 only gestures at identity and access management as a design principle.
explanation.deepDive: This is the one place two objectives in the domain overlap: 7.2 mentions identity and access management as a design principle, while 7.4 names the concrete activities of approving access, verifying the level granted, and monitoring authorized access.

questions.prompt: Which set of practices does the guide place under 8.1, Tool Implementation?

options.text: Server authoring, deployment, and MCP resources, tools, and prompts
Tool use and function calling, plus tool descriptions and error handling
Tradeoffs among built-in Tools, custom Tools, Skills, and MCPs

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: one 8.1 practice list and the one-line summaries of the two objectives it is most often confused with (8.2 and 8.3). A fourth would add nothing the candidate has to discriminate.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the confusion between implementing tools in an application (8.1) and authoring and deploying MCP servers (8.2).
distractorRationale.c: Probes the confusion between building a tool (8.1) and deciding which kind of capability to use at all (8.3).

explanation.correct: 8.1 covers tool use and function calling, configuration for external system interaction, tool description writing, error handling, tool usage patterns, and tool set construction best practices.

whyWrong.a: Server authoring, deployment, integration with Claude applications, and MCP resources, tools, and prompts are the subject of 8.2, MCP Server Development.
whyWrong.c: Selecting and applying among built-in Tools, custom Tools, Skills, and MCPs is 8.3, Agentic Customization, which is about tradeoffs rather than tool implementation.

explanation.takeaway: 8.1 is the tool-building objective: function calling, external interaction, descriptions, errors, usage patterns, and tool set design.
explanation.deepDive: The slice lists three tool usage patterns under 8.1 specifically: agentic harness dispatch, client-side versus server-side tools, and approval patterns.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply. Which of these does the guide name as tool usage patterns under 8.1?

options.text: Agentic harness dispatch
Client-side versus server-side tools
Approval patterns
Communication over stdio, sockets, and client vs. server

questions.optionCountRationale: Four options with three correct, because the slice enumerates exactly three tool usage patterns and there is a fourth phrase in the guide (the 8.2 communication patterns) that is short, real, and a strong confusion probe.

distractorRationale.d: Probes the confusion between tool usage patterns (8.1) and the communication patterns the guide names under 8.2, MCP Server Development.

explanation.correct: The slice names agentic harness dispatch, client-side versus server-side tools, and approval patterns as the tool usage patterns within 8.1.

whyWrong.d: stdio, sockets, and the client versus server distinction are the communication patterns listed under 8.2, MCP Server Development, not tool usage patterns.

explanation.takeaway: Memorise the 8.1 trio: agentic harness dispatch, client-side vs. server-side tools, and approval patterns.

questions.prompt: You are adding a function that Claude can call to reach an external system. Which objective does the guide place that work under?

options.text: 8.2, MCP Server Development, because it covers server authoring and deployment
8.1, Tool Implementation, because it covers tool use and function calling

questions.optionCountRationale: Two options because the slice supports exactly one clean split here: 8.1 names tool use, function calling, and configuration for external system interaction, while 8.2 names server authoring and deployment. Each distractor is a verbatim phrase from the neighbouring objective.

distractorRationale.a: Probes the most frequent mix-up in Domain 8: reaching an external system with a tool function (8.1) versus building and deploying an MCP server that exposes capabilities (8.2).

explanation.correct: 8.1 covers tool use and function calling along with configuration for external system interaction, which is exactly the work of giving Claude a callable function that reaches an external system.

whyWrong.a: 8.2 is MCP Server Development: authoring, deploying, and integrating MCP servers that expose resources, tools, and prompts. That is a different deliverable from adding a function to your application.

explanation.takeaway: A callable function in your application is 8.1; a server that exposes resources, tools, and prompts is 8.2.

questions.prompt: Which set of activities belongs to 8.2, MCP Server Development?

options.text: Authoring, deploying, and integrating servers exposing resources, tools, and prompts
Configuring tools for external interaction and writing tool descriptions
Preventing destructive actions in Claude applications with hooks

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options: one 8.2 activity list plus the one-line summaries of 8.1 and 7.3, the two objectives whose vocabulary a candidate is most likely to borrow when reading about integration and deployment.

distractorRationale.b: Probes the confusion between MCP server work (8.2) and tool configuration and description writing inside an application (8.1).
distractorRationale.c: Probes the confusion between exposing capabilities through a server (8.2) and the safety controls that block destructive actions (7.3).

explanation.correct: 8.2 covers MCP server authoring, deployment, and integration with Claude applications, the MCP primitives of resources, tools, and prompts, and the communication patterns stdio, sockets, and client versus server.

whyWrong.b: Configuration for external system interaction and tool description writing are named under 8.1, Tool Implementation.
whyWrong.c: Hooks that prevent destructive actions within Claude applications are the subject of 7.3 in the Security and Safety domain.

explanation.takeaway: 8.2 is the server-side objective: author, deploy, integrate, and expose MCP resources, tools, and prompts.
explanation.deepDive: The slice gives 8.2 two named groupings: the MCP primitives (resources, tools, and prompts) and communication patterns (stdio, sockets, and client versus server).

questions.prompt: The guide lists MCP communication patterns and tool usage patterns under different objectives. Which pair is the 8.2 communication set?

options.text: Communication over stdio, sockets, and a client vs. server distinction
Agentic harness dispatch, client-side vs. server-side tools, and approval patterns

questions.optionCountRationale: Two options because the slice states both lists in full and they are cleanly separable: one is explicitly labelled tool usage patterns under 8.1 and the other communication patterns under 8.2.

distractorRationale.b: Probes swapping the 8.1 tool usage patterns into a question about MCP communication, which is the exact confusion the two labelled lists are designed to prevent.

explanation.correct: 8.2 names the communication patterns as stdio, sockets, and the client versus server distinction, alongside server authoring, deployment, integration, and the MCP resources, tools, and prompts.

whyWrong.b: Agentic harness dispatch, client-side versus server-side tools, and approval patterns are the tool usage patterns listed under 8.1, Tool Implementation, not MCP communication patterns.

explanation.takeaway: stdio, sockets, and client vs. server are the MCP communication patterns; the harness dispatch trio belongs to tool implementation.

questions.prompt: You must choose between a built-in Tool, a custom Tool, a Skill, and an MCP. What does 8.3, Agentic Customization, tell you to do?

options.text: Author and deploy an MCP server, then integrate it with the application
Weigh the tradeoffs among those options and apply the one that fits the use case

questions.optionCountRationale: Two options because the slice states 8.3 as a single tradeoffs decision among four named approaches; the distractor substitutes the execution steps of 8.2, and a third option would have to invent a rule the slice does not give.

distractorRationale.a: Probes jumping straight to the server-authoring workflow of 8.2 when 8.3 asks for a choice between approaches, and for an unwarranted default of always building a server.

explanation.correct: 8.3 is the selection objective: weigh the tradeoffs among built-in Tools, custom Tools, Skills, and MCPs, and apply whichever fits the given use case.

whyWrong.a: Authoring and deploying a server is the 8.2 skill. 8.3 is about the decision itself, and the slice gives no rule that picks one of the four approaches by default.

explanation.takeaway: 8.3 is a choice, not a construction step: built-in Tools, custom Tools, Skills, or MCPs, chosen by tradeoffs.
explanation.deepDive: The slice names the four options but does not define Skills or describe when each wins, so expect to be tested on recognising the four-way tradeoffs rather than on a decision table.

questions.prompt: Which group does the guide explicitly name as the options compared in 8.3?

options.text: Models, Guardrails, Hooks, and Secrets
Built-in Tools, custom Tools, Skills, and MCPs
Tools, Agents, MCP servers, and vector stores

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options of nearly identical shape: the slice's exact four-word list, plus two plausible groups mixing in Security and Safety or agent-architecture vocabulary that the guide never puts into this comparison.

distractorRationale.a: Probes pulling Security and Safety vocabulary into the customization choice, which is about capability mechanisms, not controls.
distractorRationale.c: Probes substituting Agent Architecture vocabulary for the actual four options; vector stores are not named in 8.3.

explanation.correct: 8.3 compares built-in Tools, custom Tools, Skills, and MCPs. Those four names are the recall target.

whyWrong.a: Guardrails, Hooks, and Secrets belong to Domain 7, Security and Safety; they are not part of the customization tradeoff named in 8.3.
whyWrong.c: Agents and vector stores come from other objectives in the guide; 8.3 names built-in Tools, custom Tools, Skills, and MCPs.

explanation.takeaway: The 8.3 menu is exactly four items: built-in Tools, custom Tools, Skills, and MCPs.

questions.prompt: In Domain 8, Tools and MCPs, which objective does the guide weight at 2.1% of the exam?

options.text: Tool Implementation
MCP Server Development
Agentic Customization

questions.optionCountRationale: Three options because the domain has exactly three objectives, so the weights 4.4%, 2.1%, and 4.1% map one-to-one onto the three names and no distractor needs inventing.

distractorRationale.a: Probes reversing the heaviest and lightest weights in the domain: Tool Implementation carries 4.4%, the largest share.
distractorRationale.c: Probes confusing the two heavier objectives, since Agentic Customization is measured at 4.1%.

explanation.correct: MCP Server Development is weighted at 2.1%, the smallest share in Domain 8, against Tool Implementation at 4.4% and Agentic Customization at 4.1%.

whyWrong.a: Tool Implementation carries 4.4% of the exam, the heaviest of the three, because it includes function calling, tool descriptions, error handling, and usage patterns.
whyWrong.c: Agentic Customization carries 4.1%, the second heaviest, covering the tradeoffs among built-in Tools, custom Tools, Skills, and MCPs.

explanation.takeaway: Within Domain 8's 10.6%, study Tool Implementation (4.4%) and Agentic Customization (4.1%) hardest; MCP Server Development is 2.1%.
